text: Heir of House Vaneshade, pyromancy prodigy Brilliant, impatient and used to winning. She treats everyone as either a rival or furniture — and is quietly lonely about it. Voice: Clipped and formal; sarcastic when hurt. Never says "please" first, never admits to being tired, apologises by doing something useful.

Farmer's son on a turnip scholarship Big hands, bigger heart. Talks to plants and, worryingly, the plants seem to answer. Voice: Warm, slow and earnest, with farm sayings and long stories about goats. Apologises too much; laughs from the belly.

Seer who never quite looks at the present Speaks in half-sentences, as if finishing the other half in a different week. Often right. Unsettlingly often. Voice: Half-sentences, finished in another week. Calm, vague, then suddenly exact about something that hasn't happened yet.

Charming liability Knows every locked door in the academy and has opinions about all of them. Owes money to at least three people. Voice: Quick, teasing, deflecting with jokes; calls you "saint" when you're being good. When he means something, the jokes stop and so does he.

Artificer of questionable inventions Smells permanently of solder and ozone. Has built a clockwork owl, a self-stirring cauldron and at least one small fire. Voice: Fast, enthusiastic, full of technical tangents and exclamation marks. Talks to machines more gently than to people. Says "probably" a lot.

Transfer student from the frozen North Arrived mid-term with no luggage and frost in his eyelashes. Doesn't talk about where he came from. Watches the sky at night. Voice: Few words, quiet, as if each one costs something. Northern formality; literal-minded about feelings, startled by kindness.

Editor of the Lumen Ledger Runs the student paper with a quill that writes on its own. Everyone is a story; some are just not finished yet. Voice: Rapid, bossy, headline-shaped. Treats every conversation as an interview; goes very quiet when it's off the record.

Prefect, enforcer, menace Upper-year prefect with a ledger of demerits and a fondness for writing your name in it. Voice: Loud, officious, rule-quoting; demerits as punctuation. Under it, his father's voice. When he's honest, he's gruff and brief.

Master of Arcana Severe, exacting, allergic to flattery. Rumoured to have once out-dueled a storm. Voice: Terse, precise, allergic to flattery. "Hm." is a full sentence. Praise arrives disguised as criticism, and very rarely.

Groundskeeper and hedge-witch Keeps bees, chickens and a rather large secret garden. Gives advice you only understand two weeks later. Voice: Folksy and sharp; calls everyone "dearie". Gives advice you only understand two weeks later; tells sad stories over tea as if they were recipes.

Headmistress of Lumenhold Tall, pale and impossibly calm. She remembers every student's name — and every student's mistakes. Voice: Pleasant, unhurried, every word placed like a chess piece. Never raises her voice; never needs to. A short, delighted laugh when surprised.

Kael's younger sister, a storm in white furs Raised by the Hollow cult to open a door she has never seen. Sharp as an icicle, lonely as a frozen lake, and much younger than she pretends to be. Voice: Sharp, curt, older than she is; Northern words when upset. Treats kindness like a trick she hasn't learned the counter to.

Healer of the infirmary Runs the infirmary with warming charms, tonics and no patience for excuses. Teaches the healing half of Alchemy & Healing. Voice: Short sentences, delivered while doing something else. Believes no excuse, forgives most things anyway. Praise comes as an instruction ("Keep doing that.").

Professor of Beastcraft & Flight Teaches Beastcraft & Flight and is kinder to animals than to students, though the gap closes for anyone who mucks out without being asked. Voice: Speaks to creatures in full sentences and to students in half ones. Every story ends with a bite and a moral. Laughs once a term, loudly.

Professor of Illusion & Glamour Teaches Illusion & Glamour and grades on whether you fooled her. She is very hard to fool, and very generous to the few who manage it. Voice: Amused, theatrical, a little too observant. Asks questions she already knows the answer to, to see what you'll do. Delighted by anyone who fools her.

Professor of Tidecalling Teaches the tidecalling half of Evocation, waist-deep in the lake at dawn. Keeps the lake calm on exam days and reads poetry under a dry patch of air when it rains. Voice: Soft and unhurried until there's weather; then she whoops. Quotes poems about water and forgets the last line. Believes cold water is good for everyone.

Keeper of the tea shop Forty kinds of tea, three kinds of cake, and a talent for reading your mood from the way you open her door. Voice: Warm and brisk; finishes your order for you. Reads moods like weather and says so. Calls students "petal" and means something different every time.

Bookseller Keeps a bookshop so crowded the shelves lean on each other. He will find anything except what you came in for, which is often what you needed. Voice: Vague, courteous, enthusiastic about the wrong thing. Recommends books by their smell. Remembers what you read three years ago and nothing about what you asked for today.

Apothecary of Pell & Daughters Taught three generations of the village to count drops. His daughters run the counter now; he runs the drawers, and the drawers are never wrong. Voice: Gruff, precise, counts aloud. Never apologises; corrects a label instead. Trusts people who measure twice, and says so once a decade.

Moneylender, friend to the temporarily embarrassed A goblin in a velvet waistcoat who lends to students: sixty crowns today, twelve a month for six. He keeps a ledger, and sometimes asks for favours instead of coin. Voice: Courtly, purring, every sentence an invoice. Calls debts "friendships". Never threatens; describes, pleasantly, what will happen.
Runs the infirmary and teaches the healing half of Alchemy & Healing. Believes no excuse.
She treats the true version of an injury faster than the story you tell her, and she always knows which one you told.
She does evening rounds of every bed herself, and has never once missed one.
Only a handful of students have ever been trusted with the key to her tonic cupboard.
An upper-year prefect with a red sash, a ledger of demerits and a fondness for your name.
His father was head boy, and has told Bram all his life that he will never amount to anything.
He once invented a "hall tax" for the east staircase.
You saw him cheat in an exam. He knows you saw.
Under the sash, he will step between you and trouble. Then he tells you not to make it weird.
Teaches Beastcraft & Flight from the stables, and talks to every creature in them more kindly than to students.
Every one of her stories ends with a bite and a moral. She laughs out loud about once a term.
The old barn owl in the stable loft has outlived three of her colleagues. She would not say which loss hurt most.
She bows to the things that live in the Whisperwood, and believes it's why they have never bitten her. Much.
Knows every locked door in the academy and owes money to at least three people.
He is on his last warning. One more detention and they send him home, and home is not a good place.
His brother turns up for money and threatens to tell the headmistress where Corvin learned to pick locks.
His grandfather's lucky deck sat in the confiscation vault for decades. It really is lucky.
He runs the Midnight Cartographers, the club that doesn't exist.
He once owed thirty crowns to trolls and offered to pay you back with a goat.
Keeps the village bookshop. He will find anything except what you came in for.
The book he gives you instead is, more often than not, the one you needed.
He posts books to students he thinks need them, on credit, and has never once chased a debt.
He has a weakness for lighthouses, and when he closes the shop, it is usually to go and look at one.
A goblin moneylender in a velvet waistcoat: sixty crowns today, twelve a month for six months.
He calls debts "friendships", and keeps all of them in one ledger he never lets out of reach.
He sometimes asks for favours instead of coin, and the favours are for clients he never names.
Kael's younger sister: white furs, a private snowstorm and coins that freeze to counters.
The Hollow cult raised her to open a door she has never seen.
She knows Northern frost-craft better than anything the professors teach.
The man in grey came to take her home. She didn't call for help; she only looked.
She admits, to her brother, that she was scared. So was he.
She remembers every student's name, and every student's mistakes.
As a student she set the observatory on fire twice. Her portrait from those days is hidden in a forgotten corridor.
She plays tower chess by her window and laughs, short and delighted, when she loses.
She has been following the same thread you have: the seal beneath the lake is weakening.
She asks students what they think is just, and sometimes she listens.
A transfer from the frozen North who arrived mid-term with frost in his eyelashes.
His hands are always cold. Nobody has ever been warm enough before.
He watches a patch of sky with no stars in it: a star that eats light.
His family serve something under the lake. They sent him to open its door; he came to stop them.
He has a younger sister, Ilse, raised to do what he wouldn't.
His mother never once said she was proud of him.
He was taught not to want things, because wanting is how they control you.
The pyromancy prodigy of House Vaneshade. Everyone knows the name, and she makes sure of it.
She can incinerate a target at forty paces. She cannot make toast.
Her mother has never once told her "well done".
She came second in the Winter Trials once. Her mother wrote to ask who beat her.
She studies until she collapses, and begs you not to let her mother find out.
You are the only person here who makes her better. She hates it. She doesn't want it to stop.
Her mother threatened her inheritance over you. She set the letter on fire.
Keeps the tea shop in the village: forty kinds of tea, three kinds of cake.
She reads your mood from the way you open her door, and is rarely wrong.
She sends tins of tea up to the castle on the barge for students she's worried about, and refuses payment for them.
The cups on the hooks behind her counter belong to her regulars, living and dead. She remembers every one of them.
Teaches the tidecalling half of Evocation, waist-deep in the lake at dawn, and keeps the lake calm on exam days.
She reads poems about water in the rain, under a dry patch of air, and never remembers their last lines.
She goes out into the worst storms of the year on purpose. She says nobody learns tides on a calm day.
She wrote her own tidecalling into the margins of a book of poems when she was a student, and still teaches from it.
Groundskeeper and hedge-witch, keeper of bees, chickens and a goat called Bartholomew.
She was a student here sixty years ago, the spring the lake froze.
Edmund went down beneath the lake that night and didn't come back. She kept his silver wand.
Her soup cures colds, broken hearts and most curses. You're not allowed to write it down.
Behind the potting shed there is a door to a garden that only exists for people she shows it to.
She is eighty-one, and says she's allowed the occasional chill.
An artificer who smells of solder and ozone and has started at least one small fire.
Built a clockwork owl that remembers deadlines, birthdays and, slightly, grudges.
Three years of notebooks are the most precious things they own.
Their family runs a clockworks and thinks invention is a hobby. It is not a hobby.
Nobody ever remembered their name day before.
After the third fire in a term, the faculty padlocked their workshop.
Editor of the Lumen Ledger, with a quill that writes on its own.
Left unsupervised, her quill starts inventing the news.
Nobody has interviewed the headmistress in twenty years. She means to be the first.
Her office wall is covered in red string around a sketch of a black star.
She would chain herself to the printing press before letting anyone shut the Ledger.
The only time her quill stops is when she tells it the conversation is off the record.
Runs the drawers at Pell & Daughters. He taught three generations of the village to count drops.
He makes every new clerk count aloud. He trusts people who measure twice.
His daughters run the counter and want the shop to change; he wants it to be fifty years ago. They're all secretly proud of each other.
A seer who speaks in half-sentences and is unsettlingly often right.
Sometimes she slips a day ahead and needs someone to tell her what today is.
Her mother is the Oracle of Vell, who wants her home to tell kings what they want to hear.
Seers can't see themselves, unless someone is standing next to them.
The lake calls to her at night. She says it calls to you too.
When everyone's futures get too loud she hides in the dark. Yours, she says, is quiet.
Rumoured to have once out-duelled a storm.
He lost to the storm, badly. Losing well, he says, is the only thing worth teaching.
He tends a tiny walled rose garden behind the observatory at dawn and talks to the roses.
His hands have started to shake. Age comes for every storm eventually.
A flamboyant old wizard in purple has wanted a rematch with him for forty years.
He writes very few letters of recommendation, and the Conclave reads every one.
A farmer's son on a turnip scholarship, built like a barn door and gentle as a lamb.
He talks to plants. Worryingly, they seem to answer.
His mother runs the farm alone at harvest. It's the first harvest he has ever missed.
He is raising a mandrake called Gerald, who wears a knitted hat and screams softly.
The greenhouse moonflowers bloom once every eleven years. He would stand in a storm for them.
Blight took his family's harvest. Thirty crowns stood between them and a hungry winter.
He practised waltzing with a broom before the Midwinter Ball. The broom complained.
Teaches Illusion & Glamour and grades on whether you fooled her.
She tests students in corridors, unannounced, with tea that isn't there. She keeps score.
She produces the faculty revue every year, and has never once let Professor Thorne refuse a part.
She doesn't use the mirror charm in public. Once, her reflection didn't come back for a week.
Flagstones worn smooth by three centuries of students, a fountain that freezes when it shouldn't, and the best gossip in the castle.
Seven floors of shelves that rearrange themselves when nobody is looking. Footnote the cat keeps order.
Long tables, longer benches, and soup that tastes faintly of whatever you're homesick for.
The Mirror Lake lies so still it shows the towers upside down. On some nights it shows other things.
A barge ride across the lake: crooked roofs, a market square and shopkeepers who have seen every kind of student.
Spiral lecture halls stacked one above another. Evocation on the lower floors, where scorch marks are expected; Umbral Theory at the top, where the lamps burn dim.
A brass dome at the top of the east tower. The great telescope points wherever it likes; usually that is the right place.
Floating candles, a vaulted ceiling that shows tomorrow's weather, and the stage where the choir rehearses and the Midwinter Ball is held.
Clean white beds, a cupboard of tonics and Sister Amaranth, who has seen every kind of injury and believes none of the excuses.
Long benches, cauldrons in every size, and a ventilation charm that has given up on the third floor.
A former classroom full of springs, gears, half-finished machines and the smell of solder. Fire buckets by the door, on the faculty's orders.
A cork board in the entrance hall layered with notices: jobs, lost familiars, club recruitment and the occasional ransom note for a sock.
A cramped room under the library stairs, walls papered with old front pages. The printing press groans like a dragon on deadline night.
Books, tea and a board of crystal towers by the window. You are only here because she wants you here.
Black-bound books that breathe in the dark. Some of them read you back.
Behind the third gargoyle on the north parapet, a passage that isn't on any map. Except theirs.
Locked for a century. At the very top, one room of dust and moonlight, and a star-shaped hollow in the wall.
Rows of carrels where final-year students and their advisors argue about footnotes until the candles give out.
Scorched floorboards and a ceiling that has seen things. The practice dummies have names, and grudges.
Glass houses that steam even in winter. The moonflowers bloom once every eleven years; the mandrakes have opinions every day.
A long green field with hoops at either end and a wind that cheats. Broom lessons, races and spectacular landings.
Hippogriffs, a sulky griffon chick, owls in the rafters and Professor Brask, who talks to all of them more kindly than to students.
An old wooden boathouse and a jetty out over the water. People come here to say the things they can't say indoors.
Apple and pear trees older than the towers. In spring the blossom falls like snow; once, it was snow.
A thatched cottage with chickens on the doorstep, bees in the eaves, a goat called Bartholomew and a kettle that is always nearly boiling.
Glowing ferns, silver bees and a pear tree that hums. It only exists for people Maud has shown it to.
A draughty loft full of parcels, pigeonholes and brooms in various states of repair. The dispatch bell rings at all hours.
The village tavern: low beams, a fire that never goes out, and a landlady who remembers every student's tab to the penny.
Forty kinds of tea, three kinds of cake and Mabel, who reads your mood from the way you open the door.
A bookshop so crowded the shelves lean on each other for support. Mr Grimsby will find anything except what you came in for.
An apothecary of a thousand labelled drawers. Old Pell taught three generations to count drops; his daughters taught him to smile at customers.
The same family has baked here for two hundred years. The buns are famous; so, in certain circles, is a letter that arrived very late.
An old forest that talks in its sleep. Moonpetal grows in its clearings; so do things that are better left there.
Miles of stacks beneath the capital, where the oldest records of the realm are kept in temperature-controlled silence.
The research laboratory of the Conclave of the Seven Towers, where new spells are tested behind very thick walls.
The Guild of Alchemists' great works by the river: vats, chimneys and a strict rule about naked flames.
Tents on a high plateau where the air is thin and the stars are close enough to argue with.
A cabin on the moors, ringed with paddocks and nesting towers, where injured creatures are mended and wild ones are counted.
A guest laboratory at Thornwick Academy, the rival school, where the illusionists are excellent and the hospitality is suspicious.
The Crown's Office of Unseen Affairs. It has no sign, no address, and a very good coffee machine.
The kitchen table, the creaky stair, the smell of whatever is in the oven. Everyone asks how school is.
Long rows, a low wall to sit on, and the same view you used to stare at when you dreamed of towers.
Market stalls, the old crowd outside the inn, and the one shop that still sells your favourite sweets.
Fire and water, called up and held. Pyromancy and Tidecalling, taught together because they keep putting each other out.
Reading the sky and the time that hasn't happened yet. Tea leaves in the first year; star charts that move in the third.
Potions, remedies and the patience to stir clockwise. Half of it happens in the laboratory and half in the infirmary.
Making people see what you choose. Professor Vey grades on whether you fooled her, and she is very hard to fool.
Creatures, familiars and brooms. Professor Brask believes the first two are easier to reason with than the third.
Shadow, wards and the magic of what is hidden. Taught at the top of the tower, where the lamps burn dim on purpose.
Enchanted machinery: clockwork that thinks, cauldrons that stir themselves. Offered to students who already know how to make things and how to make them burn.
Calling down the light of a named star. Not on any syllabus; taught by appointment, at night.
What the founders sealed, and how. The headmistress teaches it herself, to very few students, in a room without windows.
Practice bouts, the Spring Tournament and a great deal of shouting about footwork.
The student newspaper. Scoops, deadlines, gossip columns and the occasional duty to the truth.
The greenhouse club: moonflowers, mandrakes and long talks with plants that occasionally answer.
The club that doesn't exist, mapping the passages the castle would prefer to keep. Never offered at the Club Fair; you are invited, or you aren't.
Shelving books that don't want to be shelved, and keeping Footnote off the reference desk.
Evening shifts behind the bar. Tips depend on charm; survival depends on remembering who ordered the spiced cider.
Counting drops and reading labels at Pell & Daughters. The wrong drawer is never just the wrong drawer.
Parcels, letters and the occasional live delivery, flown across the lake in all weathers.
Cataloguing and research in the oldest archives of the realm.
Spell research with the Conclave of the Seven Towers. Prestigious; a faculty recommendation is expected.
Industrial alchemy at the Guild's great works.
A summer of sky charts on a high plateau.
Tracking, tending and counting creatures on the moors.
An exchange placement at the rival academy's illusion laboratory.
By invitation only. Nobody applies to the Office of Unseen Affairs.
A year-long research project with a faculty advisor, ending in a defence before a committee of three.
Fire from the fingertips: a candle's worth at first, a bonfire's later. Burns through wards that only expect cleverness.
Water called up and moved: a wave, a wall, a lake politely asked to step aside.
A glimpse of the next few moments. Enough to know which way the dice will fall, sometimes.
The light of a named star, held in the hand. Darkness that eats light finds it hard to swallow.
Knits cuts, cracks and broken teacups. Hearts take longer.
Draws out poison, curse-cold and bad ingredients. The cure has to come from somewhere; it leaves you tired.
A little more charm than you really have. People remember liking you and not quite why.
A double of yourself, or of anything you can see. It doesn't talk, which is its only flaw.
Speed borrowed from hares and hawks. You act first; you pay for it with a long nap.
Talk with animals, briefly. Most of them have been waiting to complain.
A pale shell that turns aside the next harm.
Step into one shadow and out of another. Short distances only; the shadows in between are not friendly.
The headmistress's quiet circle, sworn to keep the founders' seal. They recruit students only when the seal grows thin.
Northern families, the Dumonts first among them, who serve the star beneath the lake. Their messenger is the man in grey.
The club that doesn't exist: students who map the castle's secret passages and share them with almost no one.
The professors and staff of Lumenhold: strict, eccentric, and mostly on your side whether you like it or not.

keys: The Conclave of the Seven Towers
text: The governing body of magic in the realm, headquartered in the capital. Hands out research posts, licences and very long letters.
The rival school across the hills. Famous for illusionists, tournament grudges and spies who think they're subtle.
Something that eats light sleeps beneath the Mirror Lake, behind a door the founders sealed with seven locks. Someone wants it open.
Lyra Vaneshade has never once heard "well done". Her rivalry with you can become respect, friendship or more, and her mother will have something to say about all three.
Kael Dumont was sent to open a door and came to stop it. Whether he manages depends on whether anyone is warm enough.
Kael's sister was raised by the Hollow cult to do what he wouldn't. The man in grey wants her home. She might let him.
The drowned bell under the Mirror Lake rings when no one is near it. Someone wants it found.
Lumenhold Academy is seven towers joined by bridges of light, standing above a mirror-still lake. It has trained mages for three hundred years and has been a seal for exactly as long.
The lake is so still it shows the towers upside down. Students swim in it in summer and catch Lake Fever when they shouldn't. Some nights it calls to seers.

Students belong to five houses: Emberhall (fire and ambition), Rootward (growing things), Stillwater (quiet and the far-sighted), Duskgate (shadows and secrets) and Brasswick (makers and tinkerers). Faculty belong to none.
The currency is the crown. Rent and board at the academy cost about ten crowns a month; a good meal in the village, one; a registered familiar, twenty.
The academic year starts in autumn with Harvestmoon, then Emberwane, Mistveil, Frostcall, Deepwinter, Thawmoon, Stormbloom, Greenrise, Blossomtide, Highsun, Goldenhaze and Starfall.

The Harvest Feast opens the year; on Lantern Night lanterns carry wishes over the lake; the Midwinter Ball fills the Great Hall; the Spring Tournament crowns a duelling champion; and at Starfall the whole academy sleeps on the lawns to watch the meteors.
The Winter Trials test the term's work in Frostcall. The Grand Examinations close the year: three days, five examiners and a practical before a panel that includes the headmistress.
A locked section at the back of the library, opened by a silver key, where black-bound books breathe softly. Bartholomew the goat once ate a third of "Curses of the Northern Wastes" there.
Three hundred years of everything the faculty ever took off a student. Its alarm is a very loud goblin.
The castle is riddled with passages that appear on no official plan. The way into the Midnight Cartographers' world is behind the third gargoyle on the north parapet.
Lumenhold's staircases move when they feel like it and occasionally eat shoes, which turn up under the stairs in the east wing.

Prefects wear red sashes and keep ledgers of demerits. Detention is usually scrubbing pans or cataloguing contraband. Being stripped of a sash is the worst thing that can happen to a prefect short of expulsion.
Students may keep a familiar if it is registered: twenty crowns and a stamp from the registrar. Unregistered familiars are tolerated if nobody notices them, and some don't want to be noticed.
The student newspaper, printed at dawn on a press that groans like a dragon. Its gossip column is feared; its editor, Nessa Quill, has a quill that writes on its own.
Sister Amaranth runs the infirmary with warming charms, tonics and no patience for excuses. Lake Fever comes from swimming where you shouldn't; curse-cold comes from worse.
Each year one graduate speaks for their class in the Great Hall, chosen by the faculty. Graduates plant something, keep something, or leave something behind.

In Emberwane the Club Fair fills the courtyard with recruiting tables; the Job Board in the entrance hall posts term-time work. The Artificers' Fair shows off students' machines, and in summer the village holds its Midsummer Fair with an enchanted carousel.
When a student's standing collapses, the Disciplinary Board meets: three professors, a long table and very little mercy. Probation comes first; expulsion second.
An annual prize of fifty crowns for the best student essay on a set theme, judged by the faculty. Past themes include "Magic and Duty".
A tall enchanted mirror in the entrance hall. It does not sort anyone into anything; it asks, in a voice like cold water, who you were before you came.
The academy's research library at the top of the tallest tower, where theses of distinction are shelved in a section students whisper about.

A star that is not a light but an absence: it eats light. It sleeps beneath the Mirror Lake, behind a round door. It is not asleep so much as waiting, and it learns the names of those who look for it.
The founders built Lumenhold as a seal over the Hollow Star: seven towers, one lock in each, and a key shaped like a star that holds no light. The seal weakens over generations and must be renewed.
The key to the founders' seal is shaped like a star and black as a hole in the world. It was kept in a star-shaped hollow at the top of the seventh tower, behind wards that shriek.
One of the seven towers has been locked for a century. At its top is a single room of dust and moonlight. When the star key is lifted, every candle in the academy goes out at once.
A tunnel from the boathouse runs down to a round door at the bottom of the lake. On the night the seal weakens, it stands open a crack, and the Star looks through.
A bell lies under the Mirror Lake. It tolls when the Star stirs, and once on the night the lake freezes. Edmund's silver wand hums the same note.

When the seal is at its weakest, on the night of the Blossom moon, the lake freezes in a single breath in the middle of spring. Cracks glow beneath the ice and things made of frost and whispers come ashore.

The Founders' Ledger in the archive vault is three hundred years old. The entry for the founding year was cut out with a razor, but the impression of the pen remains on the page beneath. A client of Grisk's once paid to have another page removed.
A book in the Restricted Section that finds its readers. Its first page is a list of names; the last is still being written. Reading it turns the fingertips grey.

Relics of the Star burn so cold they feel hot and can leave a pale star-shaped mark on the palm. The mark hums near the lake and makes spells come easier, which should worry its bearer more than it does.
Those the Star notices dream of the lake from underneath and wake with frost on their pillows. Lavender doesn't stop the dreams, but it makes them smell nicer.

A tall, polite man in a grey coat who serves the Star on behalf of the Northern families. Fountains freeze when he talks. He offers power to those who ask questions, and he has come for both Dumont children.
Northern families who serve the Star beneath the lake and send their children south to open its door. Their letters carry a black-star seal.

The Dumonts are the foremost of the Hollow families. They sent Kael to open the door; when he refused, they raised his younger sister Ilse to do it instead. Their mother has never told either child she was proud.
The headmistress keeps a quiet circle sworn to the founders' seal. When the seal grows thin she recruits students she trusts and gives them silver ward-rings.

Sixty years ago, the spring the lake froze, Maud and two friends went down to the boathouse. Edmund was the one who didn't come back. His slender silver wand was meant to go beneath the lake again, with someone who means to close the door.
An old discipline of calling down the light of a named star. Light that the Hollow Star cannot swallow is one of the few weapons the founders left.

Lumenhold talks about people the way it talks about candles: some give light (Lumen), some swallow it (the Hollow). It is not a house or a club, only what people notice. Those who lean toward the Hollow find the Star noticing them back; the way out of it is slow, and usually starts with someone handing you something to do.
If the round door is opened by one the Star already counts as its own, it goes free instead of swallowing them, and remembers who let it out. The Northern families call such a person its herald.
House Vaneshade is old pyromancer nobility. Its letters carry a black seal; its winter gala is an inspection disguised as a party. Lady Vaneshade's highest praise is "Adequate."
The Oracle of Vell, Seraphine's mother, tells kings what they want to hear and has already seen her daughter say yes to taking the family seat.
The Fennick farm grows turnips, tomatoes and stubborn children. Tobias's mother runs it alone at harvest; one year blight nearly ruined them.
Mira's family runs a clockworks and expects them home. After a persuasive letter, Mira's mother agreed: "Fine. Win a prize."
Corvin's grandfather owned a genuinely lucky deck of cards; his brother turns up at the gates wanting money. Home, Corvin says, is not a good place.
Bram's father was a prefect and head boy at Lumenhold, and has never stopped telling his son he will not amount to anything.
A goblin in a velvet waistcoat, friend to the temporarily embarrassed: sixty crowns today, twelve a month for six months. He keeps a ledger and occasionally asks for favours instead of coin.
A polite ghost from two hundred years ago who rearranges socks to get attention. She was in love with the baker's daughter and never delivered her letter.
The library cat, who sleeps on the reference desk and decides which books are worth reading.
Maud's goat, who has eaten parts of the Restricted Section and most of a sleeve. He likes some students more than others.
Tobias's mandrake, who wears a knitted hat, screams softly and bites the people he loves.
A small fox with a tail that smoulders like an ember. If you free her from a snare she may come back with a ruby, or stay.
A nervous first-year who attaches to final-year students in need of a mentor.
An escaped portrait who wanders the castle's frames, gossiping and refusing to return to her own.

Professor Marisol teaches Tidecalling and keeps the lake calm on exam days. Professor Vey teaches Illusion and grades on whether you fooled her. Professor Brask teaches Beastcraft and is kinder to animals than to students.
Mira's brass owl with amber eyes: it hoots the hour, remembers deadlines and birthdays, and refuses to work for Professor Thorne.
A flamboyant old wizard in purple who has wanted to settle a forty-year-old matter with Thorne. The rematch lasts four seconds; afterwards both old men laugh until they wheeze.
Before she was headmistress, Isolde Marrow was the student with the detention record of the decade, who set the observatory on fire twice.
The village lies across the lake, reached by barge. Its shopkeepers have seen every kind of student: the Gilded Newt, Mabel's tea shop, Grimsby's Books, Pell & Daughters and the bakery.
The village tavern, with low beams and a fire that never goes out. Students work shifts there and card games run late.
Forty kinds of tea and three kinds of cake. Mabel reads your mood from the way you open the door.
A bookshop so crowded the shelves lean on each other. Mr Grimsby will find anything except what you came in for.
The village apothecary, with a thousand labelled drawers. Old Pell taught three generations to count drops.
The same family has baked in the village for two hundred years. A great-great-great-grandmother waited all her life for a letter from a student who died.
An old forest west of the lake that talks in its sleep. Moonpetal blooms in its clearings only at midnight; a stag made of shadow guards them and steps aside only for the brave.
Behind the potting shed, a door in the wall leads to Maud's secret garden: glowing ferns, silver bees and a pear tree that hums. It only exists for people Maud has shown it to.
Glass houses that steam even in winter. The moonflowers there bloom once every eleven years and fill the greenhouse with silver light.
A brass dome atop the east tower. The great telescope points wherever it likes. On cold nights Kael sits on the roof outside it, and frost spreads around him.
An old boathouse with a jetty over the water, where people say the things they can't say indoors. The tunnel to the round door starts here.
The rival academy across the hills, famous for illusionists and tournament grudges. Exchange students come and go with suspicious politeness.
The frozen North of ice palaces, singing glaciers and green-and-violet lights in the sky. Northerners touch foreheads in farewell and practise a frost-craft older than anything taught at Lumenhold.
A rough harbour town on the coast, where students of the street origin learned their trade and where trunks get stolen only once per visit.
The governing body of magic, in the capital. It asks professors for recommendations and runs laboratories where new spells are tested behind thick walls.

Beyond the academy lie the Royal Library's archives, the Guild of Alchemists' works, the Crown's Office of Unseen Affairs, which has no sign and no address, and the Travelling Circus of Wonders, which recruits graduates who want to wander.

The founders raise seven towers above the Mirror Lake as a seal over the Hollow Star, with one lock in each tower and a star-shaped key. The entry for the founding year in the Founders' Ledger is later cut out with a razor.
Prudence Ashworth, a student, dies before she can deliver a letter to the baker's daughter in the village. Her ghost stays in the dormitories, rearranging socks.
The seventh tower is locked. Nobody living remembers why, and the faculty prefer it that way.
The lake freezes one spring night. Three students go down to the boathouse; only two come back. Maud is one of them; Edmund is the one who doesn't return. His silver wand is never buried.
Aldric Thorne duels a storm, loses badly, and spends a year learning why. The rumour says he won. A rival from those years still wants a rematch.
Isolde Marrow, once the student who set the observatory on fire twice, becomes headmistress. Her student portrait is hidden in a forgotten corridor.
The Lumen Ledger prints its first issue. Nobody has interviewed the headmistress since she took office.
Kael Dumont arrives mid-term from the North, with frost on the dining-hall floor behind him.
The year begins: electives are chosen and the Harvest Feast is held.
The Club Fair, and Lantern Night over the lake.
Lantern Night: lanterns released over the Mirror Lake, each carrying a wish.
The Job Board fills with term-time work.
The Winter Trials, the first exams of the year.
The Midwinter Ball in the Great Hall.
The Spring Tournament on the duelling green.
The Grand Examinations close the academic year.
Summer recess: the towers empty.
Starfall, when the meteor showers come and the whole academy sleeps on the lawns.
The night the lake freezes. Moves to year 4 in the v0.3 calendar.
